newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Almaty power project on track - Belgium's Tractebel.
newsitem.headline: Almaty power project on track - Belgium's Tractebel.

text.p: After 100 days and countless difficulties, the power generation project run by Belgian utility holding company Tractebel in the Almaty province of Kazakhstan is on track, the firm said on Thursday.

Thermal power generation output has risen from 400 megawatts when the firm took over the power stations in late August to around 600 MW now and will reach 700 MW by the end of the year, project head Nicolas Atherinos told Reuters.
Coal stocks have also been built up from 30,000 tonnes, or just three days' supply, to 800,000 tonnes against major logistical problems that needed government assistance to overcome, he said.
Almost as important, Almaty Power Consolidated (APC), the Tractebel subsidiary that runs the plants, has managed to persuade people and businesses to start paying their bills.
"When we went there it was a post-Soviet state-run enterprise with a lot of inherent problems," Atherinos, senior vice president of Tractebel's Electricity and Gas International division, said.
He said it had been a major operation organising and securing the delivery of coal from the other side of the massive central Asian republic.
"Even getting supplies of oil, which is less difficult than coal, you have to order many times the amount you need in order to get the quantity you want," Atherinos said.
"You pay, say, $50 a unit and then someone else offers, say, $55 and you suddenly find your rail tanker wagon gets diverted."
Getting people and businesses, used to a state-run system for half a century, to pay their bills, was an equal headache.
"We had to launch a tough campaign to get people to pay their bills...and had to cut off a lot of light industry," Atherinos said. "Without the help of the government we would not have succeeded."

Matters were not helped by neighbouring Russia to the north and Kyrgyzstan to the south in September suddenly disconnecting their electricity supplies to the Kazakh grid, triggering blackouts all over the country.
In order to prevent the Almaty grid being sucked dry, APC was forced itself to disconnect from the rest of the country.
Even then it had to institute selected power cuts, with its own thermal and hydroelectric power generation capacity still falling some 150 MW below demand at peak times.
That, however, is now in the past. APC signed last week contracts with Kyrgyzstan to reconnect part of the power grid and make up the difference at peak times.
"We do not now envisage having to make power cuts in the foreseeable future," Atherinos said.
